summary: Pupils (age 11+) move from knowing isolated angle facts (angles at a point sum to 360°, angles on a straight line sum to 180°, vertically opposite angles are equal) to CHAINING those facts across a single not-to-scale diagram to find several unknowns, and to writing and solving an equation for an unknown angle. The core discipline: name the fact that licenses every step (reason from geometrical structure, not from how the diagram looks or from F/Z mnemonics), keep the 'whole' explicit (180° for a line, 360° at a point) for line/point calculations, and hold apart the two relationships at a crossing — vertically opposite angles are EQUAL (found by equality, not subtraction), adjacent angles are SUPPLEMENTARY.
misconceptions: Treating vertically opposite angles as supplementary (subtracting from 180 to find the opposite angle)
Over-generalising that all four angles at a crossing are equal
Using the wrong whole — 360° where 180° applies, or vice versa
Measuring or reading the not-to-scale diagram instead of deducing from facts

activities.title: Chaining angle facts across a not-to-scale crossing
steps: Work from a not-to-scale diagram: two straight lines crossing at a point, with one of the four angles marked 130°, and a third ray splitting the opposite angle into two parts, one marked 40°.

(a) Find the three unmarked angles at the crossing. For each, write the exact fact you used (e.g. 'vertically opposite angles are equal', 'angles on a straight line sum to 180°'). Then check that the four angles at the crossing total 360° (angles at a point sum to 360°).
(b) Find the remaining part of the split angle, carrying the already-found angle forward as a given.
(c) Two vertically opposite angles are labelled (2x+10)° and 130°; write an equation and solve it for x.

Before calculating, name which relationship applies: for an angle on a line or at a point, say the WHOLE (a straight line is a half-turn 180°, a point is a whole turn 360°) and take the unknown as the whole minus the known parts; but for a vertically opposite angle the unknown is simply EQUAL to its given partner, NOT whole-minus-parts.
Write each found angle onto the diagram so it becomes a visible given for the next step.
activities.insight: Unknown angles are deduced by combining named facts in a chain, where one result feeds the next; a vertically opposite angle is found by equality while line/point unknowns are found by subtracting from the whole, and the not-to-scale picture cannot be measured, so only the facts license the answer.

activities.title: Hinged sticks: why opposite is equal and adjacent is supplementary
steps: Model a crossing with two hinged sticks (or two rulers pinned at a point).

Open the crossing wider and watch the angle you are opening and the one directly opposite it: observe that they grow TOGETHER and appear to stay equal (the hinge illustrates this; the straight-line facts explain why they must be exactly equal).
At the same time watch an adjacent angle: as one opens the neighbour shrinks, and each adjacent pair still sums to 180°.
State in words why the two opposite angles must be equal, and why an opposite pair cannot both be found by 'take it from 180'.
Contrast with a clearly non-perpendicular crossing where the two sizes are obviously different, to check that NOT all four angles are equal — only opposite pairs are.
Optional screen version: drag one ray so the linked opposite angle updates equal in real time while the adjacent value updates to keep the pair summing to 180°.
activities.insight: At a crossing there are two distinct relationships held apart: vertically opposite angles are equal, adjacent angles are supplementary — they cannot both be 'subtract from 180'.

activities.title: Introducing the vocabulary on a labelled crossing
steps: On a static crossing-lines diagram, identify the vertically opposite pair and state the relationship: equal.
Identify an adjacent pair and state the relationship: sum to 180°.
Where available as a reveal, tap an opposite pair to confirm 'equal' and an adjacent pair to confirm 'sum to 180°'.
Name each of the four angles and say which relationship each neighbour has to it.
activities.insight: The vocabulary — vertically opposite (equal) versus adjacent (supplementary) — is attached to the right pairs on a crossing before any multi-step problem is attempted.

activities.title: Quick checks: spot the supplementary-for-opposite trap and match steps to reasons
steps: Fill in a missing angle given one angle at a crossing or on a straight line.
Answer a multiple-choice item for the angle vertically opposite a given one, where one option is the supplementary value (180−x) — choose the equal value and reject the trap.
Match each found angle in a worked solution to the exact fact that justifies it.
Set a slider or chosen value for one angle and state the resulting opposite and adjacent angles.
activities.insight: These recognition and matching items are intended to rehearse the equal-versus-supplementary distinction and the habit of naming a reason; they check isolated facts rather than demonstrate a mastered multi-step chain.

checkQuestion: Give the child a NOT-TO-SCALE diagram: two straight lines crossing at a point, with one of the four angles marked 130°, plus a third ray splitting the angle opposite into two parts, one of which is marked 40°. Set them to: (a) find the three unmarked angles at the crossing and, for each, say the fact they used; (b) find the remaining part of the split angle; then (c) here two vertically opposite angles are labelled (2x+10)° and 130° — write and solve an equation for x. Watch whether they treat the opposite angle as equal or as 180 minus, whether they name a reason at each step, and whether they carry found angles forward rather than measuring the picture.
checkAnswer: For (a): the angle vertically opposite 130° is 130° (vertically opposite equal); the two adjacent angles are 50° each (angles on a straight line sum to 180°). For (b): the split angle totals 130° (vertically opposite the 130°), so the remaining part is 130−40 = 90°. For (c): 2x+10 = 130 (vertically opposite equal), so 2x = 120, x = 60. Each step is justified by a named angle fact, not by measuring.
